title: Vietnam pays the price for its trade success
gist: Vietnam ran the world's largest first-half trade surplus with the US at US$114 billion, ahead of Mexico (US$103bn) and China (US$74bn), while facing an effective US tariff of about 6% versus China's 23% — a success that now makes Hanoi a target, with transshipment allegations (which the author says are grossly exaggerated, since over 70% of Vietnam's export value is non-China) and US-style alignment clauses colliding with Vietnam's formal non-alignment.

themes.theme: The surplus that became a liability

insights.claim: Vietnam ran the world's largest trade surplus with the United States in the first half of 2026 at US$114 billion, ahead of Mexico at US$103 billion and China at US$74 billion, against US$123 billion for all of 2024.
insights.so_what: Vietnam's full-year 2026 surplus is on track to roughly double 2024 — the single number most likely to trigger a US tariff action against Hanoi.
insights.locator: Trade figures released in late August showed
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Vietnam is the fifth-largest exporter of goods to the US while importing relatively little from it, which structurally locks in a large bilateral imbalance.
insights.so_what: The imbalance is structural, not cyclical, so it cannot be negotiated away by purchase commitments of realistic size.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Hanoi's surging surplus is simultaneously the symptom of its success and its vulnerability, because under this US administration a lumpy trade surplus alone suffices to draw Washington's ire.
insights.so_what: Tariff risk now tracks the bilateral balance directly rather than any policy misconduct — screen exporters by surplus size, not by practice.
insights.quote: In this administration, a lumpy trade surplus is more than sufficient to raise Washington’s ire.
insights.locator: Hanoi’s surging trade surplus is symptomatic
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

themes.theme: Why Vietnam won the China+1 shift

insights.claim: Vietnam, alongside Mexico, has been the primary beneficiary of the shifting US tariff regimes targeting China since 2018, with its effective US tariff rate hovering at about 6% in June 2026 against China's 23%.
insights.so_what: A 17-point effective tariff differential is the quantified size of Vietnam's relocation advantage — and the size of what it loses if Washington narrows the gap.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Vietnam's other advantages are largely endogenous — low labour costs, a dense network of free trade agreements, comparatively pro-business policies and proximity to southern Chinese supply chains — making it the favoured China+1 for Korean, Japanese, Western and Chinese multinationals alike.
insights.so_what: Endogenous advantages survive tariff changes, so a tariff shock would slow rather than reverse the relocation trend.
insights.locator: Vietnam’s other major advantages are mostly endogenous
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Samsung, producing electronics and particularly mobile phones across Vietnamese plants, has consistently accounted for more than 10% of Vietnam's total exports.
insights.so_what: Single-company concentration above 10% of national exports makes Vietnam's trade data and Samsung's capex decisions mutually predictive.
insights.locator: These factors have combined to make Vietnam a favoured “China +1”
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

themes.theme: Data centre exposure and tariff carve-outs

insights.claim: Vietnam's role in electronics supply chains, primarily at final assembly, has let it profit as a picks-and-shovels supplier to the data centre boom, with Foxconn recently setting up data centre component manufacturing there.
insights.so_what: Vietnamese export growth is now partly an AI-capex derivative — a channel through which a data centre slowdown would hit Vietnam's trade and currency.
insights.quote: making a motza serving as picks and shovels suppliers for the data centre boom
insights.locator: Vietnam’s critical role in electronics supply chains
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Machinery, electronics and appliances comprise over 60% of Hanoi's exports to the US, and the White House's increasingly labyrinthine trade regime exempts many of those categories from tariffs.
insights.so_what: Most of Vietnam's US-bound value currently sits in exempted categories, so headline tariff rates understate protection — but removal of those carve-outs is the real tail risk.
insights.locator: Machinery, electronics and appliances comprise over 60%
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: China accounted for around 40% of Vietnam's US$395 billion of imports in the year to August, but a significant portion of that is Chinese capital and intermediate goods consumed by Vietnamese factories rather than goods passing through.
insights.so_what: The 40% import share is the statistic used to justify transshipment claims and the one that most needs decomposing before acting on it.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: A Lowy Institute analysis found more than 70% of Vietnam's exports reflect non-China sources, including value produced in Vietnam itself and in other countries along the supply chain.
insights.so_what: The value-added evidence undercuts the rules-of-origin case against Vietnam — a factual asymmetry that argues US claims are negotiating leverage rather than analysis.
insights.quote: While some transshipment undoubtedly occurs, its prevalence has been grossly exaggerated.
insights.locator: As one Lowy Institute analysis found
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Framing Vietnam as a mere pit stop for repackaging Chinese goods ignores a central thrust of its new growth strategy, which builds on successes in sectors like furniture by fostering deeper local supply chains.
insights.so_what: Domestic content deepening is Hanoi's policy direction, which over time strengthens its defence against origin-based tariffs.
insights.locator: Specious notions of Vietnam serving as a mere pit stop
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: A US customs team conducted spot inspections of Chinese-owned factories in Vietnam in July, and Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang visited Washington in the last week of August to revive bilateral trade deal negotiations.
insights.so_what: Physical factory inspections signal enforcement intent regardless of deal progress — a compliance cost and disruption risk for Chinese-owned plants in Vietnam.
insights.locator: In July, a US customs team visited Vietnam
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: Vietnam and the US signed a framework agreement on reciprocal, fair and balanced trade months before the Supreme Court ruled that Trump's sweeping tariffs exceeded his authority, but efforts to finalise a deal have run into disagreements over transshipment and rules of origin.
insights.so_what: Rules of origin, not headline tariff rates, is the sticking point — the clause to read when any US-Vietnam deal text emerges.
insights.locator: Months before the Supreme Court ruled
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: The US-Indonesia agreement commits Jakarta to cooperating with Washington on economic security issues like export controls and sanctions, and Washington retains the right to reinstate higher tariffs if Indonesia enters a trade agreement with a country that jeopardises essential US interests.
insights.so_what: US trade deals now embed geopolitical alignment conditions — the template that will be pressed on Vietnam and every other Southeast Asian negotiator.
insights.locator: The US–Indonesia agreement, for example, commits
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: That Malaysia, Cambodia and Indonesia — all countries arguably closer to Beijing in recent years — signed these agreements suggests the contentious alignment clauses are framed flexibly enough to be accepted.
insights.so_what: Precedent argues a Vietnam deal is achievable; the drafting flexibility, not the principle, is what determines whether it closes.
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: For reasons of geography, recent history and party ties, Hanoi is especially wary of transgressing Beijing's red lines even while deepening security ties with the US and its allies and quietly but forcefully asserting maritime claims in the South China Sea.
insights.so_what: Vietnam's constraint is tighter than Malaysia's or Indonesia's because of party-to-party ties and a shared border — expect slower, more hedged concessions from Hanoi.
insights.quote: Hanoi has been very wary of transgressing Beijing’s red lines – even while deepening security ties with the US and its allies.
insights.locator: Still, for complex reasons of geography
insights.speaker: Henry Storey

insights.claim: The coming months will test both the adroitness of Vietnamese diplomacy and the flexibility of Washington and Beijing, with alignment clauses running into Vietnam's totemic adherence to formal non-alignment.
insights.so_what: A near-dated binary: a signed US-Vietnam deal would validate Vietnam as the durable China+1 destination; failure reopens tariff risk on the world's largest bilateral surplus.
insights.locator: The following months will be a fascinating test
insights.speaker: Henry Storey
